title: When Power Makes Others Speechless
text:
In 2013 Leigh Tost, Francesca Gino and Richard Larrick reported a series of studies on what happens to a team when its leader feels powerful. In laboratory experiments, teams worked on a problem in which each member held unique information, so that finding the best answer required everyone to share what they knew. Before the task, some leaders were made to feel powerful, for example by recalling a time they had held power over others.

Teams led by leaders who felt powerful did worse. The powerful leaders talked more and dominated the discussion, and other members spoke less and felt less free to contribute. Less information was shared, and the team's decisions suffered. A field survey of real teams found a similar pattern: when leaders reported feeling powerful, open communication was weaker and team performance lower.

The researchers also found a remedy. When leaders were reminded beforehand that every member had important information and that the team's success depended on everyone's input, the harmful effect largely disappeared.
lesson: Your sense of authority can silence the very people whose knowledge you need. Talk less, ask more, and remind yourself that every person brings something you lack.
people: Leigh Plunkett Tost, Francesca Gino, Richard Larrick
source: Tost, L. P., Gino, F., and Larrick, R. P. (2013). When power makes others speechless: The negative impact of leader power on team performance. Academy of Management Journal, 56(5), 1465-1486.
caveat: Francesca Gino was later found by Harvard to have falsified data in other papers; this paper was not among those retracted, but its results deserve some care.
